articles.title: My uncle is a ghost
articles.description: In the distance, outside the window of the bedroom I grew up in, rises a tall, narrow, sleek corporate Gothic-style tower with columns of vertical windows and a grey-silver carapace. Its design, base and architect (Minoru Yamasaki) match New York's World Trade Center twin towers, just half the height. On the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, I found myself thinking about the view outside my window. The specter of 9/11 has hung over my entire life. I was born in 2005, still during the ramp-up of the War on Terror. My sister was born two months after the towers fell. On the morning of 9/11, my uncle was in the North Tower when it collapsed. The death of my uncle has always been a tricky subject to broach. Because of that, how I have processed this family tragedy - and the broader implications of the attacks of 9/11 - has always been fragmented. It has impacted all of us in our own ways. When I don't know what to think, I write. For this subject, I feel I can do neither. My uncle is a ghost. I've tried to piece together his final days. They haunt me. The week of Sept. 4, he was on vacation with his siblings, parents and my mother. In the photos, he's vivid, full of life. He jokes about life insurance at 25 for his new job. On Sept. 8 or 9, he goes back to New York early for work. That morning, he heads to the 106th floor of the North Tower for a business meeting. Finally, he feels the impact, coughs on the smoke, and emails his sister goodbye. 부모가 죽으면 산에 묻고 자식이 죽으면 가슴에 묻는다. It's a Korean proverb. When a parent dies, they are buried in the ground; when a child dies, they are buried in the heart. They never found his body. I did not know Peter; I cannot tell you how funny, popular, quirky or anything he was. But I feel him. I feel his ghost. In his images I see my father, I see myself, and I see the darkness where he is buried in my father's heart. I wonder how much of him could be buried in mine. The terror attacks of 9/11 stole from me an uncle. A man I've come to know through disparate photographs, memorabilia and stories, all now mired in a heavy layer of both nostalgia and grief. My mother would tell me stories about him, his hobbies, his sense of humor; apparently, I would have gotten along with him. My father speaks less of his late brother. Though I never met Peter, I do feel a deep sense of grief for the relationship lost. It's a difficult pain to express, a deep sense of loss for someone you never knew, but whose loss has marked my family deeply, and which now burdens me. I've seen in my family how grief can transform people and relationships. Grief doesn't simply dissipate. It moves sideways; it permeates into silence, into anger, into someone else. It can hurt. It can be passed on, but it does not go away. This pain now exists within me. A deep-seated sense of injustice, a feeling from before my birth that my family was once whole and is not now, grips us as we are now by the ghost of my uncle. Things didn't just change on 9/11; on that day, a part of our family was taken, and a piece of all of us died with his murder. My family will forever be defined in some part by that loss. It has been a difficult family dynamic to reckon with. In 1953, U.S.-backed forces in Iran launched a bloody coup d'état against Iran's Mossadegh to install the Shah and ensure Iranian oil belonged to the West. After the Gulf War, the U.S. maintained a significant military presence in Saudi Arabia to secure oil fields. Globally, America inspired fear, anger and grief. None of this is a justification for 9/11. Yet in the ensuing days, America as a country was consumed by grief. Nearly 3,000 innocents were suddenly murdered in the largest city in the most powerful country in the world. The U.S. War on Terror was an unmitigated disaster. Brown University's Costs of War Project has published that U.S. action in Syria, Yemen, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Iraq and beyond killed 4.5 million people, with roughly half of those killed civilians. From those regions, 38 million more were displaced. After 20 years, 4 presidents and $7 trillion, America packed up and went home. It did not achieve its objectives. These numbers are hard to grasp; more so is the suffering American action in the Middle East brought about. A single death is a tragedy; a million deaths are a statistic. My uncle is a statistic. One drop in the bucket of a forever war from which nobody reigns victorious. His death scars me, wounds me, leaves me searching for answers where there are none. And to see his killing co-opted, warped, twisted into a cry for hate hurts even more. He is a victim of xenophobia, hatred and malice. But he is also a victim of American greed and exceptionalism. On 9/11, America reaped what it had sown for decades. In the wake of the attacks, that sense of loss was leveraged, compounded. Our leadership beat the drums for war, choosing revenge instead of healing, offense as defense; we ourselves chose terror. That isolated and swept terror inward. America endured as we had endured, and as we were directed to endure: bravado and bluster, anger and vitriol. They say evil prevails when good men fail to act. They should say evil prevails. I wonder how many others feel a pull, feel a specter hang over their family. I think about the others who lost children, brothers, mothers on that day. I think about those flag-draped coffins of boys dead in the Middle East, buried in American hearts. I think about ruined houses in Kandahar province, those killed by a drone because of metadata and buried in Afghan hearts. None of these bring Peter back; none of them help me bury him deeper. I do not grieve righteously. I feel a grim satisfaction at Osama Bin Laden's death. But still, the ghost follows me. I cannot find it within me to forgive America, or the terrorists. But I can say we fucked up. We propagated violence. We created millions of ghosts and so much hatred. And it brought nobody back, brought no peace. I do not have a message. I am conflicted, haunted, unresolved. And I am reminded of that by something as little as looking out the window. Sebastian Alderman (they/them) is a senior from Tulsa, Okla., studying Anthropology and History on the pre-med track.

articles.title: Animate display: none in Pure CSS! Modern @starting-style & allow-discrete Explained
articles.description: For over 10 years, transitioning elements from display: none was considered impossible in pure CSS without JavaScript reflow workarounds like requestAnimationFrame or void element.offsetWidth. Those days are officially over! Modern CSS introduces two game-changing features (Baseline 2024 across Chrome, Safari, and Firefox): @starting-style: Defines the before-change style snapshot at frame 0 when an element transitions from display: none or mounts to the DOM. transition-behavior: allow-discrete: Delays flipping to display: none until your exit transitions finish completely. 💡 The Mental Model: The Broadway Stage Analogy To understand why this is necessary, think of a browser render engine like a Broadway theater: Without @starting-style: Toggling display: none to display: block is like an actor suddenly teleporting from backstage straight into a 100% bright spotlight. The browser cannot interpolate between "does not exist in the render tree" and "fully visible", so it abruptly snaps. With @starting-style: @starting-style places the actor on their backstage floor tape mark in the dark (opacity: 0, scale: 0.85) before the curtains open. Once the stage lights go up, they smoothly fade and scale into center stage. With allow-discrete: When closing, allow-discrete acts like a curtain timer. It lets the exit fade play out completely before turning off the lights and sending the element backstage. 🚀 3 Real-World Production Patterns Pattern 1: Dropdown Menus & Modals (display: none → flex) Pattern 2: Native HTML5 and ::backdrop Transitions You can animate the native element and its top-layer ::backdrop with zero JavaScript wrapper elements: dialog { opacity: 1; transform: scale(1); transition: opacity 0.3s ease, transform 0.3s ease, overlay 0.3s allow-discrete, display 0.3s allow-discrete; &::backdrop { background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65); transition: background-color 0.3s ease, display 0.3s allow-discrete; } @starting-style { dialog[open] { opacity: 0; transform: scale(0.92); background-color: transparent; Pattern 3: Dynamic DOM Elements & Toast Notifications When appending elements dynamically with JavaScript (element.appendChild), modern CSS allows them to animate on first paint automatically: 🌐 Browser Compatibility (Baseline 2024) Both @starting-style and transition-behavior: allow-discrete are part of Baseline 2024 Widely Available: Browser Supported Version Chrome / Edge 117+ ✅ Safari 17.5+ ✅ Firefox 129+ ✅ For older browser fallbacks, use @supports: 🎯 60-Second Viewer Coding Challenge How would you make a modal scale in from 90% (0.9 → 1.0) on open, but slide down 20px as it closes? Grab the spoiler-free starter HTML from our GitHub Code Vault. Write your pure CSS solution (zero JS reflow hacks!). Drop your solution in the YouTube video comments — the top 3 best solutions will be pinned and inducted into our Community Hall of Fame! 🏆 📦 Resources & Links 📺 Watch Full Explainer Video: YouTube Deep-Dive ⭐ GitHub Repository: muneebali500/cascadedev-code-vault 📄 High-Res Printable Cheat Sheet: Available inside the GitHub repo (cheat-sheet.png)

articles.title: Validating 10,000-Row CSV Uploads in 20ms Before Touching Your Server (React + IndexedDB)
articles.description: Watch someone import a 10,000-row billing CSV over spotty Wi-Fi on a standard web app. They pick the file, wait ten seconds for the progress bar to crawl to 100%, and get bounced back by a red toast: 400 Bad Request: Invalid amount on row 7,500. So they fix row 7,500, re-upload the entire file, and discover another typo on row 8,102. If their connection drops while they are editing rows in your UI and they refresh the page, things usually get worse. A lot of apps try to stash draft uploads in localStorage, forget that browsers cap localStorage around 5 MB and block the main thread synchronously on writes, and end up throwing QuotaExceededError right when the user needs a backup most. We can fix both problems on the frontend without pulling in a 200 KB validation library. In the companion repo (github.com/endlessfountain/react-offline-sheet-guard ), I wired up a small TypeScript preflight check that validates 10,000 CSV rows (40,000 cells) in 20.11 ms before a single byte hits the network, paired with a 45-line IndexedDB helper so multi-megabyte drafts survive offline refreshes. **Why naive duplicate checks freeze React tabs ** Checking whether an email looks valid or whether seatCount is an integer is cheap. The line that quietly kills browser performance on 10,000-row sheets is duplicate ID detection. When people write quick client-side validators, they often reach for Array.prototype.some() inside a row loop: typescript At 200 rows you won't notice. At 10,000 rows, scanning previousRows on every line turns into ~50 million comparisons and locks the tab for nearly a second on mid-range laptops. Swapping that array scan for a Set keeps duplicate detection O(1) per row (src/engine/sheetValidator.ts): export Notice that rowClean keeps checking all four columns on the same row instead of continue-ing after the first bad cell. If row 318 has both a broken email and "$1200" with a dollar sign, the user gets both errors at once rather than fixing the email, re-running, and getting yelled at a second time for the amount column. Running npm test in the repo generates a 418.8 KB, 10,000-row CSV with four planted errors (duplicate ID at row 50, bad email at row 500, "$1200" at row 2,500, and 3.5 seats at row 7,500): json Twenty milliseconds is barely over a single 60Hz browser frame (16.6ms), and catching those four typos upfront avoids shipping 418.8 KB over the wire on a doomed POST request. Stashing multi-megabyte drafts in IndexedDB without extra packages Raw IndexedDB has an ugly callback API from 2012, which scares people into installing wrappers or falling back to localStorage. In practice, if all you need is saving and restoring an upload draft by key, wrapping open, put, and get in Promises takes about 35 lines (src/storage/draftDb.ts): export async function saveDraftSnapshot(draft: SavedDraft): Promise { return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { tx.oncomplete = () => { db.close(); resolve(); }; tx.onerror = () => { db.close(); reject(tx.error); }; }); } In src/App.tsx, useEffect subscribes to window's "online" and "offline" events to flip a live connectivity banner and checks loadDraftSnapshot("current") on mount. You can cut your Wi-Fi in Chrome DevTools (Network -> Offline), edit the 5,000-row sample, save a snapshot, reload the tab, and pick up right where you left off. Three places where this simple setup isn't enough First, client preflight checks are purely a UX and bandwidth win, not a security boundary. Keep the exact same validation rules on your backend endpoint because anyone can send malformed payloads straight to your API with curl. Second, line.split(",") only works when none of your columns legitimately contain commas inside quotes. As soon as you add a free-text companyName column containing values like "Acme, Inc.", switch the parser step to an RFC-4180 parser such as PapaParse so quoted commas don't shift your columns right by one index.
